transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what's brought you in to see me today?

Well, hello, Doctor. I... I came in today because of the messages. You see, I play dominoes down at the park with the fellas—mostly on Tuesdays, but sometimes Thursdays if the weather's nice. Used to be we'd just play, but lately... the men at the table, they give me these little messages. Just meant for me. And it's not just them, it's the radio announcer too. I listen to the AM station, mostly for the weather, you know, because my knees ache when the rain comes. My grandfather had bad knees too, worked in the mines his whole life. Anyway, the announcer, he slips these warnings in. My wife, she tells me it's just talk, just regular broadcasting or the fellas shooting the breeze. She's always been a practical woman, makes a wonderful pot roast, but... I know what I hear. They're warning me. Telling me to be careful. I just... I don't know why they can't just say it plain, you know?
Can you tell me approximately when you first started noticing these hidden messages from the men at dominoes and the radio announcer?

Well, let's see here... when did it start? I reckon the voices and those special messages, they've been happening on and off for about nine months now. 

Nine months... you know, that's exactly how long it takes to grow a baby, which is funny to think about because my grandson's wife just had a little girl right around then. Beautiful little thing. They named her Eleanor, after my late sister. Now, my sister Eleanor, she was a real firecracker, let me tell you. She used to bake these peach cobblers that would win the blue ribbon at the county fair every single year. The judges didn't even have to taste the other folks' pies! She'd pick the peaches right off the tree in our backyard. We had a big yard back then, before they built the new highway right through the middle of town and tore it all up. The dust from those big trucks just ruined my mother's tomato plants... it was a real shame. She tried covering them with burlap, but the dirt just gets everywhere, you know? 

But, uh... what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, about nine months of the messages.
Aside from the special messages you notice in what people say or in the radio broadcasts, do you ever hear voices or sounds when no one else is around or nothing is actually being said?

Well, yes... yes, I do. Some afternoons, when my wife is out at the market and the house gets real quiet, I hear my old friend Arthur. He calls my name from the front porch. Or sometimes he'll just be humming a choir song... clear as day, like he's standing right there next to the screen door. Arthur and I, we used to sing in the choir together at the First Methodist Church. He was a baritone, had a voice like warm molasses. We'd practice on Thursday nights, and afterward, we'd go down to the diner for a slice of cherry pie. They don't make cherry pie like they used to, you know. Now it's all out of a can, too sweet, hurts my teeth. I had to get a bridge put in back in '98, cost me an arm and a leg, but the dentist—Dr. Higgins, nice fella, wore these funny bow ties—he said I needed it if I wanted to keep eating solid food. I still have to be careful with apples, though. I like a good Honeycrisp, but you really gotta slice 'em thin... 

But yes, Arthur. I hear him humming. Even though he passed on a few years back.
Have you had any recent head injuries, seizures, memory problems, or new medical illnesses—or started any new medications or substances—around the time these experiences began?

No... no, nothing like that. No head injuries or new medicines, and I've been pretty healthy, considering my age. My memory's still sharp as a tack, mostly. I mean, I can remember the exact day I bought my first car—a 1954 Ford Customline, painted a beautiful seafoam green. Oh, she was a beauty. I paid $400 cash for her, saved up from working down at the lumber yard. The smell of fresh-cut pine... there's nothing quite like it. It gets in your clothes, your hair. My wife used to make me undress on the back porch before I could come inside so I wouldn't track sawdust onto her good rugs. She bought those rugs from a traveling salesman who came through town... had a whole truck full of 'em. He wore a sharp suit, too, pin-striped. You just don't see men dressing up to do their jobs anymore, do you? Everybody's so casual now. 

But no, to answer your question, no new pills or sicknesses or anything like that. Just the same old aches and pains.

Over these past nine months, have you noticed any significant changes in your mood—like feeling unusually sad, hopeless, or on the other hand, unusually elated, energetic, or irritable—that lasted for a week or more?

Well, you know, it's funny you mention mood... because there are these weeks, and I mean a whole week or more, where I just wake up feeling so... so bright and important, you know? Like I've got the whole world figured out. I laugh real loud and I just want to talk fast, get all my ideas out. But if my wife or anyone tries to slow me down or questions what I'm saying, I get real sharp with them. I just snap. 

I snapped at my neighbor, Bill, just the other day. He was trying to tell me about his lawnmower. He bought one of those new riding ones, a John Deere, bright green with the yellow seat. Costs a fortune, those things. I told him he didn't need a riding mower for a quarter-acre lot, but he insisted. Said his knees were giving out. His knees! The man is only sixty-five. When I was sixty-five, I was still climbing up on the roof to clean the gutters myself. You gotta keep the gutters clean, especially in the fall when the oak leaves come down. We've got this massive oak tree in the front yard, must be a hundred years old. The roots are starting to lift the sidewalk, which the city says is my responsibility to fix. Can you believe that? They plant the tree, but I gotta pay for the concrete. Concrete's not cheap, either. And finding a good mason these days... they all want to rush the job, don't let it cure properly. 

But yeah, I get real irritable if folks don't keep up with me when I'm feeling that good. Just sharp as a tack, but sharp with my tongue, too.
Do you notice the hidden messages or hearing Arthur's voice happening even during the times when your mood feels normal and not especially high or irritable?

Well, yes, actually. I mean, there was... let's see, it must have been about a month ago. Things were real quiet. I was sleeping just fine, getting my solid eight hours, and I wasn't feeling all puffed up with big ideas or snapping at anybody. Just a regular, quiet month. But even then, I still heard Arthur humming on the porch, clear as a bell. And the radio, well, I still knew the announcer was slipping those special words in for me. 

Speaking of the radio, I used to have this beautiful old Philco console radio in the living room. Wood cabinet, polished mahogany. It took up half the wall, but the sound on that thing... oh, it was rich. We'd sit around it in the evenings and listen to The Lone Ranger and The Shadow. "Who knows what evil lurks in the hearts of men?" That's what they used to say. You had to use your imagination back then. Now everybody just stares at the television set. My grandson, he's got this TV that's as thin as a piece of cardboard, hangs right on the wall like a picture. I don't trust it. Seems like a strong breeze could knock it right down. And the colors are too bright, hurts my eyes if I watch it too long. But he loves it, plays his video games on it. He's a smart boy, going to college for computers. I told him he should learn a trade, learn to work with his hands. Plumbers and electricians, they'll always have work, you know? But he says computers are the future. I suppose he's right, but I don't have to like it. 

But yes, to get back to what you were asking, even when I'm feeling perfectly normal and not all wound up, Arthur's still there, and the radio still talks to me.

Thinking back over these full nine months, roughly how many weeks or months in total have you had these periods of feeling unusually high-spirited and irritable, compared to the time you've spent feeling more your usual, even-keeled self?

Well, if I look back over the whole nine months since this all started... I'd have to say that more months have been taken up by those high-energy spells, and the way I feel after them, than by my calmer stretches. It just feels like those wound-up times take over most of the calendar. 

Speaking of calendars, my wife used to buy those beautiful Norman Rockwell calendars every year. She'd hang one right by the telephone in the kitchen. We had one of those rotary phones on the wall, heavy black thing with a long, coiled cord. You could walk halfway across the kitchen while you were talking. I remember the cord used to get all twisted up on itself, and I'd have to let the receiver dangle and spin to get the knots out. People don't talk on the phone like they used to. Now everybody's walking around looking down at those little glass rectangles in their hands. The other day, I saw a young fella walk right into a parking meter because he wasn't looking where he was going. Smacked his forehead good. I wanted to tell him to put the thing in his pocket, but you can't tell young people anything these days. They think an old man like me doesn't know anything about the modern world. But I know enough to look where I'm walking, I'll tell you that much. 

But yes, to answer you... mostly those high-energy spells. They've definitely taken up the lion's share of the time lately.

And the colors are too bright, hurts my eyes if I watch it too long. But he loves it, plays his video games on it. He's a smart boy, going to college for computers. I told him he should learn a trade, learn to work with his hands. Plumbers and electricians, they'll always have work, you know? But he says computers are the future. I suppose he's right, but I don't have to like it. 

But yes, to get back to what you were asking, even when I'm feeling perfectly normal and not all wound up, Arthur's still there, and the radio still talks to me.

inference.note: Confirmation that psychotic symptoms (Arthur's voice, referential radio messages) persisted during a distinct month-long period of normal mood satisfies the criterion for psychotic symptoms occurring in the absence of mood disturbance, which is necessary for schizoaffective disorder but does not rule out schizophrenia with mood symptoms superimposed. No new information narrows between the two.

doctor.intent: Determine the total proportion of the 9-month illness period during which the mood elevation/irritability has been present, to assess whether mood symptoms have occurred for a substantial portion of the illness or only briefly relative to the psychotic symptoms
doctor.question: Thinking back over these full nine months, roughly how many weeks or months in total have you had these periods of feeling unusually high-spirited and irritable, compared to the time you've spent feeling more your usual, even-keeled self?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: Since all this started, more months have been taken up by those high-energy spells and their aftereffects than by my calmer stretches.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking to compare the total time spent in the high-spirited/irritable state (manic episodes) to the time spent feeling normal, which assesses whether the mood episodes have been present for the majority of the total duration of the illness.

patient.answer:
Well, if I look back over the whole nine months since this all started... I'd have to say that more months have been taken up by those high-energy spells, and the way I feel after them, than by my calmer stretches. It just feels like those wound-up times take over most of the calendar. 

Speaking of calendars, my wife used to buy those beautiful Norman Rockwell calendars every year. She'd hang one right by the telephone in the kitchen. We had one of those rotary phones on the wall, heavy black thing with a long, coiled cord. You could walk halfway across the kitchen while you were talking. I remember the cord used to get all twisted up on itself, and I'd have to let the receiver dangle and spin to get the knots out. People don't talk on the phone like they used to. Now everybody's walking around looking down at those little glass rectangles in their hands. The other day, I saw a young fella walk right into a parking meter because he wasn't looking where he was going. Smacked his forehead good. I wanted to tell him to put the thing in his pocket, but you can't tell young people anything these days. They think an old man like me doesn't know anything about the modern world. But I know enough to look where I'm walking, I'll tell you that much. 

But yes, to answer you... mostly those high-energy spells. They've definitely taken up the lion's share of the time lately.

inference.note: Mood episodes (manic-like irritability/grandiosity) have dominated most of the 9-month course, yet psychotic symptoms (referential messages, auditory hallucinations) persisted even during a euthymic month—meeting schizoaffective criteria (mood symptoms present majority of illness duration, with psychosis persisting >2 weeks absent mood symptoms). This pattern argues against primary schizophrenia (F20.9), which requires mood episodes to be brief/minor relative to psychotic illness duration, so F20.9 is ruled out.
